column3: It explicitly gives al-husna to those who do good, identifies them as eternal Garden-dwellers, and contrasts their unblemished state with the Fire.
The beautiful names of God share al-husna lexically, but do not address the people protected from the Fire.
God cannot be outstripped in replacing people, supplying an inverse limit on escape that sharpens the focus's prior divine allotment.
A word already given to the messengers provides a parallel for a prior divine determination, though its recipients differ.
It promises that a believer's righteous work is not denied, supplying a nearby basis for the favorable outcome introduced in the focus.
It denies that evildoers can outrun God, giving the inverse of the focus's secure removal from the final consequence.
It exposes a false claim to al-husna and assigns its claimants to Fire, contrasting them with the focus's true recipients of good.
It advances the immediate eschatological sequence toward the crisis, but adds little to the exception in the focus itself.
The foremost are named as a distinct class, a loose parallel to those for whom good has already been decreed.
Its Hell-dwellers find no escape, an inverse boundary that clarifies the focus's being kept away from it.
It immediately specifies the focus's protected people: they do not even hear the Fire and remain eternally in fulfilled desire.
It presents a mistaken perception of the event as distant, contrasting with the real distance granted to the protected.
It sets al-husna for those who answer their Lord against bad reckoning and Hell for those who do not, giving a clear criterion and contrast.
The fulfilled good promise is contrasted with a person summoned for judgment after worldly enjoyment, extending the focus's prior good toward its outcome.
The wished-for distance from a ruinous companion is a distinct but secondary image of distance revealed at arrival.
A word that has preceded from the Lord delays judgment, sharing the form of prior divine determination without the focus's salvation.
The impossibility of return for a destroyed town belongs to the local end-time movement but does not explain the protected group.
The racing agents supply only a remote parallel to precedence and add no account of good or removal from Fire.
It states that the condemned are not absent from the Fire, directly opposing the focus's distance from it.
It establishes the general fate of the addressed worshippers and their objects as fuel entering Hell, which the focus immediately qualifies by exception.
The arrogant figures are not able to outstrip God, adding a concrete inverse of the safe prior disposition in the focus.
The impotence of alleged gods to protect their worshippers supports the surrounding Fire verdict, but not the focus's positive exception.
It completes the protection described in the focus: the greatest terror does not grieve them and angels welcome them to their promised day.
No one can outstrip God's determination of death, a broad inverse of escape that is less specific than earlier parallels.
God promises al-husna to all who spend and fight, while distinguishing ranks among them; it broadens the category of a divine good promise.
The welcome from the Forgiving, Merciful One is a secondary image of the hospitable afterlife of the protected.
Distant error and punishment describe an opposing state, without specifying the focus's prior good or removal.
The hypocrites' claim to intend al-husna is exposed as false, a weaker contrast to the genuine good already assigned in the focus.
The approaching true promise and the terrified unbelievers give the immediate crisis from which the focus distinguishes its protected people.
No community can precede or delay its appointed term; the temporal limit only loosely parallels the focus's preceding good.
The unbeliever's presumptuous claim to al-husna is followed by punishment, a redundant false counterpart to earlier contrasts.
It confirms that the alleged gods and their worshippers remain eternally in the Fire, preserving the contrast that makes the focus's exception necessary.
Requested distance between journeys and ensuing dispersal use distance in an unrelated historical setting.
A prior word postpones judgment among divided people, but it does not illuminate the focus's favored recipients.
The afterlife residents receive whatever their souls desire, directly elaborating the fulfilled-desire side of the protection completed in 21:102.
Those who hasten in good deeds are foremost in them, offering an active moral counterpart to the focus's people marked by prior good.
The prior word postponing a dispute is another remote decree parallel and adds little beyond 20:129.
It describes the Fire's torment and deafening condition immediately before the focus states who are kept away from it.
Distant opposition to revelation is an adverse form of distance, but does not clarify the protected outcome.
A Garden pleasure without headache or intoxication gives only a general, redundant contrast to the Fire.
The return to idolatry after relief does not materially explain the focus's prior good or distance from Fire.
The prohibition of ridicule and abusive naming is not a substantive link to the eschatological protection in the focus.
Rejecters cannot enter the Garden, supplying a clear negative boundary opposite the focus's divinely favored group.
The cosmic folding and re-creation are part of the surrounding eschatological frame but add no specific account of the exception.
Disbelievers cannot think they have escaped God, a concise inverse of being genuinely removed from the final Fire.
The prior word delaying judgment in a dispute is too general to add to the focus.
The enduring true promise to believers provides a general afterlife confirmation, without the focus's protection-from-Fire relation.
The instruction about questions does not bear on the focus's final destination.
The righteous servants inheriting the earth continues the local positive destination and identifies a related favored servant class.
Those who give without injury have reward, no fear, and no grief, anticipating the focus sequence's freedom from final terror.
The polemic over assigning daughters to God does not clarify the focus.
The followers cannot leave the Fire, a direct inverse of the focus's being made distant from it.
The declaration is a communication for worshipping people, a nearby thematic transition but not an explanation of the exception.
The warning about hypocrisy and distorted judgment does not add to the focus's fate distinction.
The reaction to news of a daughter is unrelated to the focus.
God does not let the deeds of those killed in His way go astray, a broad preservation theme with no Fire-distance relation.
The mission as mercy to the worlds is a nearby thematic expansion, but it does not identify the people set apart in the focus.
God does not waste the reward of good work, restating the positive preservation already supplied by 21:94.
Believers who do righteous deeds have Gardens of bliss, giving a general positive destination for a group like the focus's favored people.
Believing righteous doers are the best of creation, a general qualification that is less specific than the Garden links.
The proclamation of one God turns to the audience's response but does not explain the Fire exception.
The possibility of a compelling sign from heaven does not add to the focus.
The false allocation of provision to unknown partners is unrelated to the protected group.
Blinding and racing on the path do not provide a meaningful link to the focus.
The uncertain nearness or distance of the promised event continues the local warning, without explaining why some are excluded from it.
The crowd's wish to follow victorious magicians has no material relation to the focus.
The oath by Mount Sinai does not add to the focus.
Affirming al-husna offers a secondary connection to the focus's al-husna, though the promised outcome is not stated here.
God's knowledge of open and hidden speech does not clarify the focus's protection.
Denying al-husna gives an inverse response to the good in the focus, but remains too abbreviated to add much.
Preferring worldly life does not itself explain the focus's prior divine good.
God accepts people's best deeds, overlooks their wrongs, and places them among Garden companions, providing a developed positive outcome.
The possibility of a trial and temporary enjoyment gives no specific account of the protected group.
Believers who do righteous deeds are eternal Garden companions, a redundant general parallel to 31:8.
The closing appeal for true judgment and help from the Merciful is adjacent in the surah but does not elaborate the exception.
Faith, righteous work, and humility lead to eternal Garden residence, adding a modest further qualification for the favored outcome.
Evil punishment and ultimate loss form a general contrast, but do not specifically address Fire-distance.
The warning that defrauders will be resurrected is not a substantive link to the focus.
The foremost are brought near, forming a meaningful spatial counterpart to the focus's favored people being kept far from the Fire.
Those who seek worldly life have only Fire in the Hereafter, an inverse outcome already well established by the local sequence.
The nullification of deeds and absence of helpers gives a broad adverse outcome without a direct link to the focus.
Those opposing God and His messenger are among the abased, a general negative counterpart only.
Patient righteous people receive forgiveness and great reward, adding moral traits and a favorable result for the protected class.
Believing righteous people receive forgiveness and noble provision, a redundant positive counterpart after 11:11.
The earliest believers receive divine approval and eternal Gardens, a secondary precedent-and-reward parallel.
The specified provision of God's devoted servants gives a general afterlife reward, without the Fire contrast.
Those who lower their voices before the messenger receive forgiveness and great reward, another general moral condition with limited marginal value.
Later believers ask forgiveness for those who preceded them in faith, a limited lexical parallel to prior precedence.
Faith unmingled with wrongdoing yields security and guidance, supplying a present form of the safety associated with the focus's favored group.
Unbelievers who die in disbelief cannot ransom themselves from painful punishment, an inverse outcome but not a specific Fire-distance link.
The record of the righteous is in Illiyyin, a lofty positive placement that only loosely parallels the focus's good allotment.
The diversity of human striving does not specifically explain the focus.
The rebuke for worshipping Baal rather than the best Creator does not add to the focus.
The question to former idolaters is not a substantive addition to the focus.
The warning against following desires after revelation does not clarify the favored group or its outcome.
The marriage prohibitions do not bear on the focus.
The rule concerning retaliation and divine aid is unrelated to the focus.
The inheritance allocations do not bear on the focus.
The signs of resurrection are only a remote eschatological background and add no marginal clarification here.
The parable of an ungrateful town's worldly deprivation does not explain the focus's final protection.
Whoever is kept away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has succeeded, stating the focus's separation from Fire in its clearest outcome form.
Avoiding grave sins brings expiation and admittance through a noble entrance, supplying a concise condition-and-entry parallel.
It sets the opposing boundary: associating partners bars the Garden and makes the Fire one's refuge, clarifying the exception after 21:98.
The good people are greeted by angels at death and told to enter the Garden for their deeds, anticipating the welcome in 21:103.
After the universal approach to it, God saves the God-fearing and leaves the wrongdoers there, closely paralleling the focus's removal from the Fire.
Purification is rewarded with Gardens of Eden and eternal residence, providing a developed positive destination for the favored.
The beings alleged to be God's offspring are instead honored servants, supplying a local distinction relevant to what may wrongly be counted among worshipped objects.
Those honored servants do not precede God in speech and act by His command, a local inverse to autonomous escape or claim.
Their intercession depends on God's approval and they fear Him, further defining the honored servants within the local contrast.
Any of those servants who claimed divinity besides God would be repaid with Hell, sharply preserving the boundary around the exception.
The inheritors of Paradise inherit al-Firdaws and remain there, giving a focused positive counterpart to distance from the Fire.
The Garden of Eternity is promised to the God-fearing as recompense and destination, closely matching a prior divine good promise.
God's sincerely devoted servants are explicitly excepted from the condemned group, structurally paralleling the focus's exception from the Fire.
God saves the God-fearing in their success; no evil touches them and they do not grieve, directly paralleling 21:101-103's safety and freedom from grief.
Those who fear their Lord are led in groups to the Garden and welcomed at its gates, giving the arrival side of the focus's removal.
Those who say God is their Lord and remain steadfast receive angels telling them not to fear or grieve and promising the Garden, closely echoing 21:103.
God's servants are told that they will have no fear that day and will not grieve, directly matching the protected group's final security.
The believers are commanded to enter the Garden in joy, supplying the positive destination paired with the focus's distance from Fire.
The Garden contains whatever its residents desire, independently reinforcing the fulfilled-desire conclusion of 21:102.
The God-fearing are in gardens and bliss, a concise positive counterpart to the Fire's excluded inhabitants.
The one brought near receives comfort, provision, and a Garden of bliss, strengthening the spatial contrast between nearness to good and distance from Fire.
A Garden as wide as the heavens and earth is prepared for believers, described as God's bounty given to whom He wills.
Repentant believers ask not to be disgraced as their light runs before them, and are promised Gardens beneath which rivers flow.
God admits whom He wills into His mercy while preparing painful punishment for wrongdoers, giving a direct mercy-versus-punishment distinction.
For the God-fearing is attainment and gardens, supplying an explicit favorable destination for the protected class.
The most God-fearing person will be kept away from the Fire, an exceptionally close verbal and thematic parallel to the focus.
Believing righteous people receive eternal Gardens and God's approval, completing the positive outcome only partially represented by 98:7.
